subject: air-combat
title: Basic Fighter Maneuvers
objective: Understand one-versus-one BFM geometry, pursuit, turn performance, vertical maneuvering, energy and guns employment well enough to describe what each aircraft is doing and why.
applicability: Aircraft-agnostic concepts illustrated with US Navy T-45C training figures; type-specific numbers belong to that training example.

subject: airfield-operations
title: The Airfield and the Traffic Pattern
objective: Read a military airfield's runway numbers, markings, arresting gear, signs and lighting, read the Navy optical landing system and the PAPI, choose the runway in use from the wind, fly the overhead break and the standard pattern, make Navy field calls, and move safely on the ground.
applicability: Military pilots first: US Navy shore airfield practice (NAVEDTRA 14342A, VT-10 training script) as the worked example, with shared US (FAA) standards and civil towered and non-towered procedures as supplementary. Each air station's course rules and published procedures take precedence.

subject: radio-communications
title: Radio Procedures and Phraseology
objective: Speak and understand military air–ground radio: a Navy training sortie's calls, call signs and preset channels, formation check-ins and training-rule calls, then the FAA technique, phonetic alphabet and numbers, contact calls, readbacks, emergency calls, transponder codes and what to do when the radio fails.
applicability: For US military pilots: US Navy training squadron scripts and instructions first, with the FAA Aeronautical Information Manual as the supplementary US civil rule set; units, other services and other countries differ in detail.

subject: flight-fundamentals
title: Principles of Flight
objective: Understand the four forces, lift and angle of attack, drag, control and stability, turns and load factor, stalls, the maneuvering envelope and energy well enough to explain what a military jet is doing and why.
applicability: For military pilots: fixed-wing principles from Navy aerodynamics texts, with FAA handbooks as supplementary sources; worked numbers use an invented jet trainer, with US Navy T-45 training figures where cited.
